drug_name: Ethynodiol Diacetate and Ethinyl Estradiol Tablets
what_its_for: This combination birth control pill is used to prevent pregnancy. It contains two hormones — a progestin (ethynodiol diacetate) and an estrogen (ethinyl estradiol) — that work together to stop ovulation (the release of an egg), thicken cervical mucus to block sperm, and thin the uterine lining. It may also be prescribed to help regulate menstrual cycles or treat certain hormonal conditions.
how_to_take: Take one tablet by mouth at the same time every day. It is very important to take it at the same time each day to keep hormone levels steady and to get the best protection against pregnancy. You can take it with or without food. If the pill upsets your stomach, try taking it with a meal or at bedtime. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Follow the order of tablets in your pill pack exactly as directed — do not skip or rearrange them.
dosing: Take one tablet every day for 28 days (one full pack). For a 21-day pack, take one active (hormone) pill daily for 21 days, then take no pills for 7 days before starting a new pack. For a 28-day pack, take one active pill for 21 days, then take one reminder (inactive/placebo) pill daily for 7 days. Start your next pack the day after finishing your current pack — do not skip any days between packs. When starting for the first time, your doctor may tell you to start on the first day of your period (Day 1 start) or on the first Sunday after your period begins (Sunday start). Use a backup birth control method such as condoms for the first 7 days if you use the Sunday start method.
missed_dose: If you miss 1 pill: Take it as soon as you remember, even if it means taking 2 pills in one day. Then continue taking the rest of your pills at your usual time. No backup birth control is needed. If you miss 2 pills in a row in Week 1 or Week 2: Take 2 pills on the day you remember and 2 pills the next day, then continue one pill per day. Use backup birth control (like condoms) for the next 7 days. If you miss 2 pills in a row in Week 3, or miss 3 or more pills at any time: Do not try to make up all the missed pills. Throw away the rest of the pack and start a new pack that same day (Day 1 start) or start a new pack the next Sunday (Sunday start). Use backup birth control for the next 7 days. You may not have a period that month — this is normal. If you miss two periods in a row, take a pregnancy test and call your doctor. If you miss any reminder (inactive) pills, just throw away the missed ones and continue your pack — you do not need backup birth control.
storage: Store at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Do not store in the bathroom medicine cabinet where it can get hot and humid. Keep the pills in their original blister pack until you are ready to take them. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused pills down the toilet. Ask your pharmacist about the best way to dispose of any unused medication.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking, especially if you are over 35 years old. Smoking while taking birth control pills greatly increases your risk of serious heart problems, including blood clots, heart attack, and stroke. Avoid taking this medication with grapefruit juice, as it may affect how the medication works. Do not take herbal supplements such as St. John's Wort without telling your doctor, as it can make your birth control less effective. Avoid prolonged bed rest or sitting for long periods (such as long flights) since this can increase the risk of blood clots. Tell all your doctors and pharmacists that you take this pill before starting any new medications, including antibiotics, antifungals, seizure medicines, or HIV medications, as some drugs can make your birth control less effective. Avoid missing doses, as this can reduce the pill's effectiveness.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience any of the following warning signs (remember the word ACHES): Abdominal pain (sudden or severe), Chest pain or shortness of breath, Headaches that are severe or unusual, Eye problems such as blurred vision or loss of vision, Severe leg pain or swelling in one leg. Also contact your doctor if you have: Signs of a blood clot such as sudden numbness, weakness, or confusion; Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice); Severe depression or mood changes; Unusual vaginal bleeding or no period for two months in a row; Signs of a severe allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face, or difficulty breathing; High blood pressure; Breast lumps or nipple discharge; Migraines that are new or getting worse; Signs of pregnancy.
when_it_works: If you start taking this pill on the first day of your period (Day 1 start), you are protected against pregnancy right away. If you start on any other day, it takes 7 days of consistent pill-taking before you are fully protected — use a backup birth control method such as condoms during that first week. The pill is most effective when taken every day at the same time without missing any doses. It does NOT protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as HIV, chlamydia, or gonorrhea — only condoms can help prevent STIs.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use this medication if you are pregnant or think you may be pregnant. Stop taking it and contact your doctor immediately if you become pregnant. Breastfeeding: This combination pill is generally not recommended for women who are breastfeeding because estrogen can reduce milk production. Talk to your doctor about progestin-only options. Teenagers: This medication may be used by adolescents after their first menstrual period. Directions and safety are the same as for adults. Women over 35 who smoke: This medication is not recommended due to a significantly increased risk of serious cardiovascular events including blood clot, heart attack, and stroke. Women with certain medical conditions: Tell your doctor if you have or have had blood clots, stroke, heart disease, liver disease, breast cancer, migraines with aura, uncontrolled high blood pressure, or diabetes with complications, as this medication may not be safe for you. Older adults: This medication is not indicated for use after menopause.
